los.text: Describe clinical findings to the investigation and treatment of pre-eclampsia.
los.html:
Definition (NICE NG133)New hypertension (≥140/90) after 20 weeks plus proteinuria (urine PCR ≥30 mg/mmol) or other maternal organ dysfunction (AKI, raised transaminases, neurological features, low platelets/haemolysis) or uteroplacental dysfunction (fetal growth restriction).
Pathophysiology
  • Poor trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries
  • → placental ischaemia
  • → release of anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1), low PlGF
  • → widespread endothelial dysfunction (vasoconstriction, leaky capillaries, platelet activation).
FindingsDetail
SymptomsHeadache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), epigastric/RUQ pain, vomiting, sudden swelling of face, hands, feet
SignsHypertension, proteinuria, hyperreflexia/clonus, papilloedema, RUQ tenderness, oedema
BloodsFBC (platelets), LFTs (transaminases), U&E/creatinine; PlGF-based test (20–36⁺⁶ weeks) helps rule out
FetalUltrasound growth, liquor, umbilical artery Doppler, CTG
Complications
  • Eclampsia (seizures), HELLP (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), stroke, placental abruption, pulmonary oedema, AKI, DIC
  • FGR, preterm birth, stillbirth
  • Later maternal cardiovascular disease
PreventionAspirin 75–150 mg nightly from 12 weeks until birth if one high-risk factor (previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, diabetes, chronic hypertension) or two moderate (first pregnancy, age ≥40, interval >10 years, BMI ≥35, family history, multiple pregnancy).
Treatment
  • Antihypertensives: labetalol first line (avoid in asthma), nifedipine MR, methyldopa; target ≤135/85; admit if BP ≥160/110 or concerns.
  • Severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia: IV magnesium sulfate (4 g loading, then 1 g/h for 24 h; monitor reflexes, RR, sats, urine output; toxicity → calcium gluconate); IV labetalol or hydralazine; fluid restriction (~80 mL/h) to avoid pulmonary oedema.
  • Definitive cure = delivery of the placenta: deliver at 37 weeks, earlier if severe or deteriorating (antenatal steroids if <35 weeks, magnesium for neuroprotection <30 weeks).
  • Postnatal: can present up to 6 weeks after birth; continue BP checks; enalapril postnatally (safe in breastfeeding).

los.text: Describe the causes, investigations and treatment of bleeding in pregnancy.
los.html:
TimingCausesKey features
Early (<24 weeks)Miscarriage (threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed)Bleeding ± cramps; cervical os open in inevitable/incomplete
Ectopic pregnancyPain (often before bleeding), shoulder-tip pain, collapse; empty uterus on scan
Molar pregnancyVery high hCG, hyperemesis, large-for-dates uterus, "snowstorm" scan
Cervical/vaginal (ectropion, polyp, infection)Post-coital bleeding
Antepartum haemorrhage (≥24 weeks)Placental abruptionPainful, tender, woody-hard uterus, may be concealed (shock out of proportion), fetal distress; risk: hypertension, smoking, cocaine, trauma
Placenta praeviaPainless bright red bleeding, soft non-tender uterus, high or malpresenting head; no digital vaginal examination until excluded
Vasa praeviaPainless bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal distress (fetal blood)
Uterine rupturePrevious caesarean, pain, loss of contractions, fetal distress
Postpartum haemorrhage (≥500 mL; major >1000 mL)4 Ts: Tone (atony, ~70%), Trauma, Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (coagulopathy)
Investigations
  • ABCDE
  • hCG and transvaginal ultrasound (early pregnancy unit)
  • Serial hCG (rise ≥63% in 48 h suggests viable intrauterine pregnancy)
  • FBC, clotting, group and save/crossmatch
  • Rhesus status
  • Kleihauer test (size of fetomaternal haemorrhage) after 20 weeks
  • CTG and ultrasound (placental site) later.
Treatment
  • Miscarriage: expectant, medical (misoprostol ± mifepristone) or surgical (manual vacuum aspiration).
  • Ectopic: methotrexate (unruptured, small, hCG <1500, little pain), laparoscopic salpingectomy; ruptured → emergency surgery.
  • APH: resuscitate (2 large-bore cannulae, crossmatch), steroids if preterm, deliver if mother or fetus compromised; praevia → planned caesarean at 36–37 weeks.
  • PPH: call for help, uterine massage, bimanual compression, oxytocin, ergometrine (not in hypertension), carboprost (not in asthma), misoprostol, tranexamic acid; then balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, embolisation, hysterectomy; major haemorrhage protocol.
  • Anti-D for Rhesus-negative women where indicated (e.g. bleeding after 12 weeks, ectopic or surgical management).

los.text: Describe the physiological changes that occur in pregnancy.
los.html:
SystemChangeConsequence
CardiovascularCardiac output ↑ ~40% (stroke volume and HR ↑), SVR ↓ (progesterone), BP falls mid-pregnancyFlow murmurs, S3; aortocaval compression when supine after 20 weeks
BloodPlasma volume ↑ 40–50% > red cell mass ↑ 20–30%Dilutional anaemia (Hb thresholds: 110 g/L first trimester, 105 later)
Hypercoagulable (↑ fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X; ↓ protein S)VTE risk 4–6×, highest postpartum; D-dimer unhelpful
WCC ↑, platelets slightly ↓Gestational thrombocytopenia
RespiratoryTidal volume ↑ → minute ventilation ↑ (progesterone), O₂ consumption ↑, FRC ↓ (raised diaphragm)Compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ ~4 kPa); breathlessness; rapid desaturation
RenalGFR and renal plasma flow ↑ ~50%Lower creatinine and urea (a "normal" creatinine may be abnormal); glycosuria; dilated ureters (right > left) → pyelonephritis risk
EndocrineInsulin resistance (hPL, cortisol, progesterone)Gestational diabetes
hCG stimulates the TSH receptor; TBG ↑Low TSH in the first trimester; total T4 ↑, free normal
Prolactin ↑, pituitary enlarges; cortisol and RAAS ↑
GIProgesterone relaxes smooth muscle; hCGReflux, constipation, delayed gastric emptying (aspiration risk), nausea (peak 8–12 weeks), gallstones; ALP ↑ (placental), albumin ↓
MSK and skinRelaxin, weight gain (~10–15 kg)Pelvic girdle and back pain, carpal tunnel; linea nigra, chloasma, striae

los.text: Recall key legal issues surrounding the area of pregnancy and childbirth.
los.html:
IssueKey point
Legal status of the fetus
  • No legal personality until born alive with an existence separate from the mother
  • It can't be a party to proceedings or be "murdered" in utero
Maternal autonomy
  • A competent pregnant woman can refuse any treatment, including a caesarean, even if the fetus will die
  • The fetus's interests don't override hers
Capacity in labour
  • Pain, fear or exhaustion don't remove capacity unless the MCA test is failed
  • If she lacks capacity, act in her best interests (Court of Protection for complex cases)
ConsentMust disclose material risks and reasonable alternatives (including caesarean) (Montgomery)
AbortionLawful only under the Abortion Act 1967 conditions (see LO 6)
Prenatal injury
  • A child born alive can sue for injury caused negligently before birth (Congenital Disabilities (Civil Liability) Act 1976)
  • a mother is only liable for negligent driving
Fertility, surrogacyHFE Acts 1990/2008 (embryo research, licensed treatment, legal parenthood); surrogacy agreements are unenforceable (Surrogacy Arrangements Act 1985); parental orders
Confidentiality, young peopleGillick competence and Fraser guidelines; safeguarding duties
FGMIllegal (FGM Act 2003); mandatory reporting to police if under 18
RegistrationBirths registered within 42 days; stillbirths (≥24 weeks) must be registered

los.text: Recall key legislation surrounding the area and of key cases that have created legal precedent in the area.
los.html:
LegislationEffect
Offences Against the Person Act 1861 (ss 58–59)Procuring a miscarriage is an offence unless within the Abortion Act (Parliament voted in 2025 to remove criminal liability for women acting in relation to their own pregnancy; check whether this is in force)
Infant Life (Preservation) Act 1929Offence of child destruction of a fetus "capable of being born alive"
Abortion Act 1967 (amended by HFE Act 1990)Defence to the above if its conditions are met; 24-week limit for most grounds
Congenital Disabilities (Civil Liability) Act 1976Claims for prenatal injury
HFE Acts 1990, 2008Fertility treatment, embryos, parenthood
Mental Capacity Act 2005Capacity and best interests in pregnancy and labour
CasePrinciple
Paton v BPAS (1979); C v S (1988)A father can't stop an abortion; the fetus has no legal rights
Re MB (1997)A competent woman may refuse a caesarean for any reason; MB lacked capacity (needle phobia) so treatment was lawful
St George's Healthcare NHS Trust v S (1998)Detaining a woman under the Mental Health Act to force a caesarean was unlawful
Attorney General's Reference (No 3 of 1994) (1998)
  • A fetus isn't a "person" for murder
  • Manslaughter possible if a child injured in utero is born alive and then dies
CP v CICA (2014)Drinking heavily in pregnancy isn't a crime against the fetus
Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015)Consent: disclose risks a reasonable patient would consider significant (shoulder dystocia in a diabetic mother)
McKay v Essex AHA (1982)No claim for "wrongful life"
McFarlane v Tayside (2000); Parkinson v St James (2001); Rees v Darlington (2003)Wrongful birth damages (see LO 7)
Khan v Meadows (2021)Damages limited to the risk the doctor was asked to advise on (haemophilia, not unrelated autism)

los.text: Explain the law in respect of termination of a foetus (and its legal status prior to birth).
los.html:
• Abortion Act 1967 (England, Wales and Scotland): termination is lawful if two registered medical practitioners agree in good faith (form HSA1) that one of the grounds applies, carried out by a doctor in an NHS hospital or approved place (early medical abortion pills can be taken at home up to 9⁺⁶ weeks), and notified to the Chief Medical Officer (HSA4).
GroundConditionTime limit
AContinuing the pregnancy risks the woman's life more than terminationNone
BNecessary to prevent grave permanent injury to her physical or mental healthNone
CContinuing risks her physical or mental health more than termination (~98% of abortions)24 weeks
DRisk to the health of her existing children24 weeks
ESubstantial risk that the child would have serious physical or mental abnormalityNone
F, GEmergency to save life or prevent grave permanent injury: one doctor is enoughNone
Conscientious objection(s 4)Doctors needn't participate except in emergencies, but must refer promptly (GMC); applies only to direct, "hands-on" participation (Doogan 2014).
Legal status of the fetus
  • No legal personality until born alive (Paton, C v S, Re MB)
  • Protected indirectly by criminal law (1861 and 1929 Acts) and the Abortion Act's time limits
  • The father has no right to be consulted or to prevent it.
Under 16s can consent if Gillick competent; Northern Ireland has a separate legal framework (decriminalised 2019).

los.text: Discuss legal aspects of the law surrounding wrongful birth (and the matter of clinical negligence).
los.html:
• Clinical negligence requires: duty of care, breach (the Bolam test: practice accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion, which must be logically defensible (Bolitho); for consent, Montgomery), causation ("but for"; Chester v Afshar for failure to warn) and damage within the scope of the duty (Khan v Meadows).
ClaimExampleDamages
Wrongful conceptionFailed sterilisation or vasectomy
  • Healthy child: no costs of upbringing (McFarlane v Tayside 2000)
  • Damages for pregnancy and birth
  • a conventional award (Rees v Darlington 2003)
Wrongful birthMissed anomaly on scan, failure to offer screening, so parents lost the chance to terminateDisabled child: the extra costs of the disability are recoverable (Parkinson v St James 2001)
Wrongful life (the child's own claim that it shouldn't have been born)Not recognised (McKay v Essex AHA 1982)
Prenatal injuryNegligent care causing injury (e.g. hypoxic brain injury in labour)Child's claim (1976 Act); maternity claims are the NHS's largest cost (cerebral palsy)
Limitation3 years from the date of knowledge; for children, 3 years from their 18th birthday.
WalesPutting Things Right (NHS Redress (Wales) Measure 2008) allows redress up to £25,000 without court; duty of candour.

los.text: Describe how to interpret genetic tests
los.html:
TestWhat it tells you
Combined test (11–14 weeks: nuchal translucency + hCG + PAPP-A + age)Chance of trisomy 21, 18, 13; "higher chance" if ≥1 in 150; it's screening, not diagnosis
Quadruple test (14–20 weeks: AFP, hCG, uE3, inhibin A)If too late for the combined test
NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood)
  • Offered after a higher-chance result
  • ~99% detection for T21 but still screening (false positives from confined placental mosaicism): confirm with an invasive test before acting
CVS (11–14 weeks) / amniocentesis (from 15 weeks)Diagnostic; ~0.5% miscarriage risk
QF-PCRRapid aneuploidy result (2–3 days)
Karyotype, chromosomal microarrayStructural changes, copy number variants
Exome/genome sequencingSingle-gene causes of fetal anomalies
Patterns
  • Down syndrome: ↑ NT, ↑ hCG, ↓ PAPP-A (quad: ↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ uE3, ↑ inhibin A)
  • Edwards/Patau: hCG and PAPP-A both low.
Interpreting results
  • Predictive value depends on prevalence (the same test gives more false positives in a low-risk population)
  • Mosaicism
  • Variants of uncertain significance (don't act on them)
  • Incidental findings.
Carrier screening
  • Sickle cell and thalassaemia (family origin questionnaire)
  • If the woman is a carrier, test the partner (25% risk for an autosomal recessive condition if both carry).
InheritanceAutosomal dominant 50%; X-linked recessive: half of a carrier mother's sons affected, half her daughters carriers; penetrance and variable expressivity.
CounsellingNon-directive, explain chance vs certainty, options (further testing, continuing, termination), support.

los.text: Identify the indications and procedure of operative delivery.
los.html:
Assisted vaginal birth (forceps, ventouse)
IndicationsProlonged second stage (delay), suspected fetal compromise, maternal exhaustion, shortening the second stage for maternal medical reasons (cardiac disease, severe hypertension)
PrerequisitesFully dilated cervix, membranes ruptured, cephalic with position known, head ≤1/5 palpable abdominally, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, consent, experienced operator, back-up plan
ChoiceVentouse: less maternal trauma, not before 34 weeks; forceps: more successful, more perineal (anal sphincter) injury
ComplicationsPerineal tears, PPH; baby: cephalohaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage (ventouse), facial nerve palsy, scalp/facial marks
Caesarean section
Elective indications
  • Breech (after failed ECV)
  • Placenta praevia
  • Previous caesareans (or choice)
  • HIV with high viral load
  • Primary genital herpes in the third trimester
  • First twin non-cephalic
  • Maternal request
Urgency categories
  • Cat 1: immediate threat to life of woman or fetus (decision-to-delivery ≤30 min)
  • Cat 2: compromise not immediately life-threatening (≤75 min)
  • Cat 3: needs early delivery, no compromise
  • Cat 4: elective
ProcedureRegional (spinal) anaesthesia usually; antibiotics before incision; Pfannenstiel skin incision; lower segment transverse uterine incision; oxytocin; VTE prophylaxis
RisksHaemorrhage, infection, VTE, bladder/bowel injury; future placenta praevia/accreta, uterine rupture in later labour; transient tachypnoea of the newborn

los.text: Describe the variety of presentations seen in pregnancy
sessions: Twins and abnormal lie (Inc. breech delivery)
los.html:
PresentationThink of
Nausea and vomiting
  • Normal (peak 8–12 weeks)
  • Hyperemesis gravidarum (>5% weight loss, dehydration, ketosis: antiemetics such as cyclizine or prochlorperazine, then ondansetron; IV fluids, thiamine, VTE prophylaxis)
  • Molar or multiple pregnancy
  • UTI
Abdominal painEarly: ectopic, miscarriage; later: abruption, labour, pre-eclampsia/HELLP (RUQ), UTI/pyelonephritis, appendicitis, fibroid degeneration, ovarian torsion, round ligament pain
BleedingSee LO 2
Reduced fetal movements (after 24 weeks)Fetal compromise: same-day CTG ± ultrasound
Headache, visual symptomsPre-eclampsia, venous sinus thrombosis, migraine
Breathlessness, chest pain, leg swellingPhysiological, anaemia, PE/DVT (leading direct cause of maternal death in the UK), peripartum cardiomyopathy
Itching (palms and soles, no rash)Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: raised bile acids; ursodeoxycholic acid for symptoms; stillbirth risk rises with very high bile acids
Fluid leakageRupture of membranes (PPROM: erythromycin, steroids)
Painful contractions before 37 weeksPreterm labour: steroids, magnesium (<30 weeks), tocolysis
Urinary symptomsUTI (treat asymptomatic bacteriuria), pyelonephritis
Thirst, polyuria, large babyGestational diabetes (OGTT at 24–28 weeks: fasting ≥5.6 or 2-hour ≥7.8 mmol/L)
Low mood, anxiety; acute confusion postnatallyPerinatal depression; postpartum psychosis (emergency)
Injuries, missed appointmentsDomestic abuse (often starts or escalates in pregnancy)

los.text: Elicit an obstetric history from a pregnant patient
los.html:
SectionContent
Presenting complaintIn her words; ICE
Current pregnancy
  • LMP
  • EDD and gestation
  • Planned?
  • Booking
  • Scans (dating 11–14 weeks, anomaly 18–20⁺⁶ weeks)
  • Screening results
  • Booking bloods (FBC, group and antibodies, haemoglobinopathy, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis)
  • Fetal movements
  • Symptoms and complications
Obstetric history
  • Gravidity and parity (e.g. G3 P1+1: three pregnancies including this one, one birth ≥24 weeks, one loss <24 weeks)
  • Each pregnancy: year, gestation, mode of birth, complications, birth weight, outcome
GynaecologicalCervical screening, contraception, STIs, fertility treatment
Past medicalDiabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, thyroid, VTE, heart disease, previous surgery
Mental healthPrevious depression, bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis (high risk)
Drugs and allergiesFolic acid, vitamin D, teratogens (valproate, ACE inhibitors, warfarin, isotretinoin)
Family historyPre-eclampsia, diabetes, genetic conditions, twins, VTE
SocialSmoking (CO monitoring), alcohol, drugs, occupation, support, housing, domestic abuse (ask when alone), safeguarding

los.text: Perform a comprehensive antenatal examination, ensuring a thorough assessment of maternal and foetal well-being
los.html:
Maternal assessment
General: BMI, pallor, oedema, BP (correct cuff, seated), urine dip (protein, glucose), reflexes if hypertensive
Inspection: size for dates, scars (caesarean), striae, linea nigra, fetal movements
Fundal height landmarks: just palpable at 12 weeks, umbilicus ~20 weeks, xiphisternum ~36 weeks
SFH from 24 weeks (tape from fundus to symphysis, cm ≈ weeks ±2), plotted on a customised growth chart
Palpation: lie (longitudinal, transverse, oblique), presentation (cephalic, breech), engagement (fifths palpable), liquor volume
Fetal heart: hand-held Doppler (110–160 bpm); CTG if concerns
Fetal well-being
  • Fetal movements (ask: reduced movements need same-day assessment), serial SFH growth, heart rate
  • Ultrasound for growth (estimated fetal weight, abdominal circumference), liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler if SFH is small, static or high-risk.
Reporte.g. "Singleton pregnancy, longitudinal lie, cephalic, 3/5 palpable, SFH 33 cm at 34 weeks, fetal heart 140 bpm."

los.text: Identify and list potential differential diagnoses for a pregnant patient presenting with symptoms of tiredness, breathlessness, and urinary symptoms
los.html:
SymptomDifferentials
Tiredness
  • Physiological (first and third trimesters)
  • Iron deficiency anaemia
  • Hypothyroidism (or hyperthyroidism)
  • Gestational diabetes
  • Perinatal depression
  • Poor sleep
  • Infection
  • Hyperemesis/dehydration
  • B12/folate or vitamin D deficiency
  • Domestic abuse
Breathlessness
  • Physiological (progesterone-driven hyperventilation: gradual, normal sats and examination, not at rest)
  • Anaemia
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Asthma
  • Pneumonia
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy
  • Pulmonary oedema (pre-eclampsia)
  • Pre-existing heart disease (mitral stenosis)
  • Thyrotoxicosis
Urinary symptoms
  • Physiological frequency (pressure from the uterus)
  • UTI/asymptomatic bacteriuria
  • Pyelonephritis
  • Gestational diabetes (polyuria)
  • Stress incontinence
  • Retention (retroverted uterus)
  • Stones
  • Ruptured membranes mistaken for urine
Investigations
  • Obs and sats, FBC and ferritin, TFTs, glucose/OGTT, urine dip and MSU culture, ECG
  • CTPA or V/Q (with leg Dopplers) if PE suspected (don't rely on D-dimer)
  • Echo if cardiac.
Prescribing
  • UTI in pregnancy: nitrofurantoin (avoid at term), amoxicillin (if sensitive) or cefalexin
  • Avoid trimethoprim in the first trimester (folate antagonist).
  • Oral iron if Hb <110 g/L (first trimester) or <105 g/L (later).

los.text: Identify and interpret clinical signs and symptoms of thyroid disease, including hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism
sessions: Neck & Thyroid status examination and TFT interpretation
los.html:
HyperthyroidismHypothyroidism
SymptomsWeight loss with increased appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, irritability, diarrhoea, oligomenorrhoeaTiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, menorrhagia, low mood, slow thinking
SignsTachycardia/AF, fine tremor, warm sweaty skin, lid lag and retraction, proximal myopathy, brisk reflexes, goitreBradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes, dry coarse skin, puffy face, hoarse voice, carpal tunnel, goitre (Hashimoto's)
Graves'-specificExophthalmos, ophthalmoplegia, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy, diffuse goitre with bruit
CausesGraves' (TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies), toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute painful, postpartum), amiodarone, excess levothyroxine; gestational thyrotoxicosis (hCG, hyperemesis)Hashimoto's (anti-TPO), after radioiodine/thyroidectomy, iodine deficiency (commonest worldwide), drugs (amiodarone, lithium, carbimazole), pituitary disease, postpartum thyroiditis
Blood cluesHyponatraemia, high cholesterol, macrocytosis, raised CK
  • In pregnancy: untreated hypothyroidism → miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, impaired fetal neurodevelopment: increase levothyroxine (by ~25–50 µg) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
    • Hyperthyroidism: propylthiouracil in the first trimester, then carbimazole (teratogenic early)
    • TRAb crosses the placenta (neonatal thyrotoxicosis)
    • no radioiodine.

los.text: Analyze and interpret thyroid function tests (TFTs) in the context of patient history and clinical findings to support diagnosis of thyroid disorders
sessions: Neck & Thyroid status examination and TFT interpretation
los.html:
TSHFree T4 (± T3)Interpretation
HighLowPrimary hypothyroidism
HighNormalSubclinical hypothyroidism (treat if TSH >10, symptomatic, pregnant or planning)
LowHighPrimary hyperthyroidism (only T3 high = T3 toxicosis)
LowNormalSubclinical hyperthyroidism (or recovering, or excess levothyroxine)
Low or normalLowSecondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism, or sick euthyroid
Normal/highHighTSH-secreting adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance, erratic levothyroxine use, assay interference
Context
  • Sick euthyroid in acute illness (low T3, low-normal T4 and TSH): repeat after recovery
  • Pregnancy uses trimester-specific ranges (TSH low in the first trimester from hCG)
  • Drugs (amiodarone, lithium, steroids, biotin interference).
Next tests
  • Anti-TPO (Hashimoto's)
  • TRAb (Graves')
  • Technetium uptake scan (diffuse uptake: Graves'; patchy: multinodular; single hot nodule: adenoma; low uptake: thyroiditis or exogenous hormone)
  • Ultrasound for nodules.
On levothyroxine
  • Monitor TSH 6–8 weeks after a dose change
  • a high TSH suggests under-dosing, poor adherence, malabsorption (taken with calcium, iron or PPIs) or pregnancy.
